7 Visualising and Analysing Time-oriented Data

7.1 Installing packages

Use the pacman package to install and load multiple packages at once with.This ensures that all listed packages are installed (if not already) and loaded into the R session.

pacman::p_load(scales, viridis, lubridate, ggthemes, gridExtra, readxl, knitr, data.table, CGPfunctions, ggHoriPlot, tidyverse)

7.2 Importing Data

The command attacks <- read_csv("data/eventlog.csv") reads the CSV file eventlog.csv from the data folder into a tibble dataframe named attacks using the readr package.

attacks <- read_csv("data/eventlog.csv")

7.3 Examining the data structure

The below command displays the first few rows of the attacks dataset in a formatted table using the knitr package for better readability in reports.

kable(head(attacks))

7.4 Data preparation

Step 1: Deriving weekday and hour of day fields

make_hr_wkday <- function(ts, sc, tz) {
  real_times <- ymd_hms(ts, 
                        tz = tz[1], 
                        quiet = TRUE)
  dt <- data.table(source_country = sc,
                   wkday = weekdays(real_times),
                   hour = hour(real_times))
  return(dt)
  }

Step 2: Deriving the attacks tibble data frame

wkday_levels <- c('Saturday', 'Friday', 
                  'Thursday', 'Wednesday', 
                  'Tuesday', 'Monday', 
                  'Sunday')

attacks <- attacks %>%
  group_by(tz) %>%
  do(make_hr_wkday(.$timestamp, 
                   .$source_country, 
                   .$tz)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(wkday = factor(
    wkday, levels = wkday_levels),
    hour  = factor(
      hour, levels = 0:23))
kable(head(attacks))
tz source_country wkday hour
Africa/Cairo BG Saturday 20
Africa/Cairo TW Sunday 6
Africa/Cairo TW Sunday 8
Africa/Cairo CN Sunday 11
Africa/Cairo US Sunday 15
Africa/Cairo CA Monday 11

7.5 Building the Calendar Heatmaps

A calendar heatmap visualizes time-series data by mapping values to a calendar layout, helping to identify trends and patterns over time.

grouped <- attacks %>% 
  count(wkday, hour) %>% 
  ungroup() %>%
  na.omit()

ggplot(grouped, 
       aes(hour, 
           wkday, 
           fill = n)) + 
geom_tile(color = "white", 
          size = 0.1) + 
theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") + 
coord_equal() +
scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                    low = "sky blue", 
                    high = "dark blue") +
labs(x = NULL, 
     y = NULL, 
     title = "Attacks by weekday and time of day") +
theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
      legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 6) )

7.6 Building Multiple Calendar Heatmaps

Multiple calendar heatmaps display time-series data across different categories or years, enabling comparisons and trend analysis across multiple time periods.


# Load required libraries
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(lubridate)
library(ggthemes)

# Load data (modify the file path as needed)
attacks <- read_csv("data/eventlog.csv")

# Convert timestamp to date-time format if needed
attacks <- attacks %>%
  mutate(
    date_time = as.POSIXct(timestamp, format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"),
    wkday = factor(weekdays(date_time), 
                   levels = c("Sunday", "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", 
                              "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday")),  # Order weekdays
    hour = hour(date_time)  # Extract hour of the day
  )

# Identify the top 4 source countries with the highest number of attacks
top_countries <- attacks %>%
  count(source_country) %>%  # Use correct column name
  top_n(4, n) %>%
  pull(source_country)

# Filter data for the top 4 source countries
attacks_filtered <- attacks %>%
  filter(source_country %in% top_countries)

# Aggregate attack counts by weekday and hour for each source country
grouped <- attacks_filtered %>%
  count(source_country, wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  na.omit()

# Plot multiple heatmaps using facet_wrap()
ggplot(grouped, aes(x = hour, y = wkday, fill = n)) + 
  geom_tile(color = "white", size = 0.1) + 
  facet_wrap(~ source_country, ncol = 2) +  # Create separate heatmaps for each country
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                      low = "sky blue", 
                      high = "dark blue") +
  labs(x = NULL, 
       y = NULL, 
       title = "Attacks by Weekday and Time of Day") +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") + 
  theme(
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 6),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12)
  )

7.7 Plotting Multiple Calendar Heatmaps

Step 1: Deriving attack by country object

attacks_by_country <- count(
  attacks, source_country) %>%
  mutate(percent = percent(n/sum(n))) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))

Step 2: Preparing the tidy data frame

top4 <- attacks_by_country$source_country[1:4]
top4_attacks <- attacks %>%
  filter(source_country %in% top4) %>%
  count(source_country, wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(source_country = factor(
    source_country, levels = top4)) %>%
  na.omit()

7.8 Plotting Multiple Calendar Heatmaps

Plotting multiple calendar heatmaps involves generating separate heatmaps for different time periods or categories, allowing for visual comparisons of trends and patterns.

ggplot(top4_attacks, 
       aes(hour, 
           wkday, 
           fill = n)) + 
  geom_tile(color = "white", 
          size = 0.1) + 
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") + 
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                    low = "sky blue", 
                    high = "dark blue") +
  facet_wrap(~source_country, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, 
     title = "Attacks on top 4 countries by weekday and time of day") +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 6) )

7.9 Plotting Cycle Plot

A cycle plot visualizes seasonal patterns by displaying time-series data across different cycles (e.g., months or days), highlighting trends and variations within each cycle.

7.9.1 Data Import

The below command imports the Excel file arrivals_by_air.xlsx from the data folder into an R dataframe named air using the readxl package.

air <- read_excel("data/arrivals_by_air.xlsx")

7.9.2 Deriving month and year fields

Deriving month and year fields involves extracting the month and year from a date column using functions like month() and year() from the lubridate package for time-based analysis.

air$month <- factor(month(air$`Month-Year`), 
                    levels=1:12, 
                    labels=month.abb, 
                    ordered=TRUE) 
air$year <- year(ymd(air$`Month-Year`))

7.9.3 Extracting the target country

Extracting the target country means selecting or filtering data for a specific country from a dataset, using functions like filter() in dplyr to focus on relevant records.

Vietnam <- air %>% 
  select(`Vietnam`, 
         month, 
         year) %>%
  filter(year >= 2010)

7.9.4 Computing year average arrivals by month

Computing the year’s average arrivals by month means grouping data by month and calculating the mean number of arrivals for each month across all years using group_by(month) %>% summarize()

hline.data <- Vietnam %>% 
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avgvalue = mean(`Vietnam`))

7.9.5 Plotting the cycle plot

Plotting the cycle plot involves visualizing monthly trends over multiple years by grouping data by month and year, showing seasonal patterns and variations across time.

ggplot() + 
  geom_line(data=Vietnam,
            aes(x=year, 
                y=`Vietnam`, 
                group=month), 
            colour="black") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=avgvalue), 
             data=hline.data, 
             linetype=6, 
             colour="pink", 
             size=0.5) + 
  facet_grid(~month) +
  labs(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
       title = "Visitor arrivals from Vietnam by air, Jan 2010-Dec 2019") +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("No. of Visitors") +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica")

7.10 Plotting Slopegraph

A slopegraph visualizes changes between two or more points in time by connecting values with lines, highlighting trends, rankings, or comparisons across categories.

7.10.1 Data Import

rice <- read_csv("data/rice.csv")

7.10.1 Plotting the Slopegraph

Plotting the slopegraph involves drawing lines between data points across two or more time periods to highlight changes, trends, or rankings in a clear and comparative way.x`

rice %>% 
  mutate(Year = factor(Year)) %>%
  filter(Year %in% c(1961, 1980)) %>%
  newggslopegraph(Year, Yield, Country,
                Title = "Rice Yield of Top 11 Asian Counties",
                SubTitle = "1961-1980",
                Caption = "Prepared by: Priya")
